content.title: About
content.content: The multigrain bagel is a yeasted baked good that incorporates whole grains, bran, and seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, flax). It has the classic round shape with a hole in the middle, a dense crumb and a slightly crisp crust. Bagels are often sliced, toasted, and topped with cream cheese, hummus, or used as a sandwich base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Traditional preparation involves boiling the dough briefly in water with baking soda before baking, which gives the bagel its distinctive chew.
The multigrain version appeared in the 1970s as a response to growing demand for more nutritious, whole‑grain products.
In many countries the bagel is considered a "grab‑and‑go" breakfast because it is easy to eat on the move.
There are over 30 bagel varieties, ranging from raisin and cranberry to cheese and seed‑topped versions.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grains and bran increase dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Slow‑digesting carbohydrates provide steady energy and help keep you full longer.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Sunflower and pumpkin seeds add polyunsaturated fatty acids that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Grain components are rich in thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The bagel supplies magnesium, iron and zinc, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Seed allergy
items.content: Sunflower, pumpkin or flax seeds may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Some bagels are topped with coarse salt; people watching sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Made from wheat flour, bagels contain gluten and are not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added seeds and bran can make the bagel more calorie‑dense than plain bread; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel in half, toast it, and spread cream cheese, avocado, hummus or peanut butter. It works well as a sandwich with turkey, smoked salmon, vegetables and greens. Small bagel cubes can be added to salads or used as a crunchy topping for soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Before eating, warm it in a toaster or oven to restore the crisp crust.
